---
title: "FALCONAge"
---

FALCONAge is a package for scoring published aging clocks. It reads DNA methylation - as a beta
matrix, a GEO series matrix, or RRBS coverage files - and clinical chemistry as a table of blood
measurements. For each of the 161 clocks in its catalogue it matches the features that clock
needs against the ones you have, applies the transforms and coefficients the clock's paper
specifies, and returns a score per sample with what is needed to read it: the coefficient file's
digest, the fraction of features found, the device and precision it ran in, and every warning
raised on the way.

A clock returns a number on an age-like scale, and what that number means is fixed by the target
the model was fitted to. Those targets are different quantities. Horvath 2013 predicts
chronological age in years; ZhangMortality predicts a log hazard; DunedinPACE predicts a rate, in
biological years per chronological year; epiTOC2 estimates cumulative stem-cell divisions; a
deconvolution clock returns cell-type proportions. Reporting all five as "biological age" throws
away the one thing needed to interpret any of them.

So every registry entry declares a `scale_type` - one of eight - beside its unit, platform,
species and the tissue its coefficients were fitted in, and the scale type decides which
downstream operations are available. Age acceleration is a residual against chronological age: it
is defined for a clock reported in years and undefined for a rate, so FALCONAge computes it for
Horvath and raises an error for DunedinPACE rather than subtracting an age from a ratio.

## Install

FALCONAge is **not on PyPI or CRAN yet**. Both packages install from the GitHub repository, and
both live in a subdirectory of it, so the commands name that subdirectory.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python

```bash
pip install "falconage @ git+https://github.com/bhagesh-h/FALCONAge.git#subdirectory=python"
```

Pin a tag in anything you intend to reproduce - `...FALCONAge.git@v1.0.0#subdirectory=python`.
`main` moves; a tag does not.

For CUDA, install torch from PyTorch's own index first. Pip's default index serves a CUDA build on
Linux and a CPU-only build on Windows under the same name:

```bash
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124
```

### R

```r
remotes::install_github("bhagesh-h/FALCONAge", subdir = "r")
# or
pak::pak("bhagesh-h/FALCONAge/r")

library(FALCONAge)
falconage_install()    # creates the managed Python environment, once
falconage_config()     # what resolved: versions, devices, registry size
```

`falconage_install()` installs the Python core from the same GitHub tag the R package was built
from, so the two halves cannot drift.

:::

## Score something

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python

```python
import falconage as fa

data = fa.prepare(fa.read_betas("betas.csv"))
res  = fa.score(data, clocks="compatible")

res.summary()
fa.acceleration(res, method="both")
fa.plot.ba_vs_ca(res, "horvath2013")
fa.report.write_report(res, "report.html")
```

### R

```r
library(FALCONAge)

d   <- prepare(read_betas("betas.csv"))
res <- score(d, clocks = "compatible")

summary(res)
acceleration(res, method = "both")
plot_ba_vs_ca(res, "horvath2013")
report(res, "report.html")
```

:::

Both produce the same numbers, because both run the same code. The R package delegates all
arithmetic to the Python core through reticulate, and the R suite asserts equality at tolerance
exactly zero rather than approximate agreement.

## What is in the catalogue

161 clocks, in three availability tiers. The tiers are about redistribution rights, not about
whether the algorithm works - every architecture is implemented and tested regardless of tier.

| Tier | n | What you do |
|---|---:|---|
| **A** | 23 | Nothing. Twenty ship a coefficient file; PhenoAge, KDM and homeostatic dysregulation are formulas with none to ship. |
| **B** | 110 | Catalogued, but no primary source for the numbers has been established, so nothing is bundled. |
| **C** | 28 | Obtain a coefficient file and register it. The architecture is implemented and tested; the numbers are research-use-only. |

```python
fa.registry.load().filter(availability="A")
```

In R, `citation("FALCONAge")`. The machine-readable version is
[CITATION.cff](https://github.com/bhagesh-h/FALCONAge/blob/main/CITATION.cff), which is what
GitHub's *Cite this repository* button reads.

The clock FALCONAge computed for you is somebody else's work, and citing
FALCONAge does not cite it. Every registry entry carries its primary
reference, so the list for an analysis comes out of the analysis:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python

```python
fa.registry.load().get("grimage2").cite("bibtex")
```

### R

```r
cite_clock("grimage2", "bibtex")
```

:::
